warmup.q: A test runs backgroundScope.launch { probe.readings().collect { got += it } }, where readings() is a correct callbackFlow that registers a listener, and on the very next line calls probe.fire(reading). Then it calls runCurrent(). What is in got?
options: Nothing: the listener wasn't registered when the reading fired
warmup.why: On the default StandardTestDispatcher, launch only queues the collector. The callbackFlow block that calls register runs in a producer coroutine when the scheduler next runs, which is at runCurrent(), after the fire. The reading found no listener and went nowhere. Real code has the same gap.

opening:
The old wireless oven probe from the coroutines track is still in the kitchen drawer. You push it into the roast, and it calls you. Its library has a listener: you register a function, and the probe calls it on its own thread (a worker that runs code) with every new reading, until you unregister it. Next door, the neighbour's kitchen runs on Reactor, a line of stations where each one asks the one before it for a number of items at a time. And before a big dinner, the house holds a rehearsal on a fake clock.

A flow fits none of these. It waits to be collected, it hands values over by suspending, and its delays take real time. The easy trap is to wrap the probe in a few lines that work in a demo, and then lose readings, or leave the listener behind, in the first busy hour.

Hot flows in depth shared values inside one program. In this lesson, we'll bridge the probe with callbackFlow, survive the burst it sends on connect, cross into Reactor and back, and rehearse it all on virtual time. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with an old probe that calls you, a neighbour who speaks Reactor, and a rehearsal on a fake clock. callbackFlow fits a hatch to the probe: trySend fills a shelf sized for the burst, and awaitClose takes the listener down. asFlow and asFlux turn request(n) into suspension and back, and runTest and Turbine rehearse it all.

Now search your own code for callbackFlow, and check two lines in each: the awaitClose, and what happens to a failed trySend.

That ends the Flow track. Next, we'll go underneath, to the sockets where all this waiting happens. Why does a server with one thread per client run out of threads long before it runs out of work?

sections.h: A callbackFlow is a hatch between the probe and your flow
sections.html:
Here is a first bridge from the probe's listener to a flow, a recipe card for values that a collector receives by calling collect. The caller starts collecting in a coroutine (a light piece of work that can pause without holding a thread), gives way once with yield(), a pause that lets other coroutines run, and then the probe fires a reading:

Java
// Java equivalent: Flux.create runs its lambda inside subscribe(), so the listener is there at once
Flux<ProbeEvent> events = Flux.create(sink -> {
    ProbeRegistration registration = probe.register(new ProbeEventListener() {
        public void onEvent(ProbeEvent e) { sink.next(e); }
        public void onError(Throwable t) { sink.error(t); }
        public void onClosed() { sink.complete(); }
    });
    sink.onDispose(registration::unregister);
});
events.subscribe(e -> System.out.println("got " + e));
probe.fire(new ProbeEvent(0, 61));   // got ProbeEvent(seq=0, celsius=61)
Kotlin
fun DemoProbe.events(): Flow<ProbeEvent> = callbackFlow {
    val registration = register(object : ProbeEventListener {
        override fun onEvent(event: ProbeEvent) { trySend(event) }   // on the probe's thread
        override fun onError(error: Throwable) { close(error) }
        override fun onClosed() { close() }
    })
    awaitClose { registration.unregister() }
}

launch { probe.events().collect { println("got $it") } }
yield()
probe.fire(ProbeEvent(0, 61))   // fired with listeners=0

callbackFlow is a flow builder for listener APIs. Its block registers a listener that drops each value into a channel, a queue between coroutines, and the collector takes the values out on the other side. The Kotlin reading is lost. collect on a callbackFlow starts a producer coroutine, and your block, with its register call, runs inside that coroutine only when it is first scheduled. launch and one yield() got the collector going, but not its producer. Reactor's Flux.create runs its lambda inside subscribe(), on the calling thread, so the Java version has no gap. In Kotlin, collecting does not mean registered. A test must wait for the registration, and real code must not count on it.

Picture the bridge as the hatch with a shelf from Context and threads, fitted to the probe. The probe's thread puts each reading on the shelf with trySend, which never waits. send would wait for room, so it is a suspend function, one that can pause its coroutine, and calling it from a plain listener method doesn't compile: "suspension functions can only be called within coroutine body". awaitClose { } is you standing at the hatch until you're told to leave, and then taking the hatch down. It suspends until the channel closes and runs its block in a finally, so the listener goes away whatever ended the flow: take(2), a cancelled collector, close(error) from onError (the collector's collect throws that error), or close() from onClosed (the flow completes normally).

Forget awaitClose, and the library sounds an alarm as soon as the block returns with the channel still open. It is quite insistent:

java.lang.IllegalStateException: 'awaitClose { yourCallbackOrListener.cancel() }' should be used in the end of callbackFlow block.
Otherwise, a callback/listener may leak in case of external cancellation.
See callbackFlow API documentation for the details.

Reactor has no such check. A Flux.create without onDispose still has its listener registered after take(1) has finished, and nothing tells you. For your own coroutines feeding one flow, such as two thermometers that you launch yourself, use channelFlow from lesson 3 of this track: the same machinery without the check, and it completes when the block and all its children are done. For a callback that fires only once, use suspendCancellableCoroutine.

Collecting is not registering. End every callbackFlow with awaitClose.

Check yourself: the collector is cancelled while it waits for a reading. Which line of the bridge runs, and on which ending of the flow would it not run? The listener is now in place and goes away cleanly. The probe's first act on connect is to send everything it stored.

try.expect: Part 0 prints fired with listeners=0, and registered only after it, so the collector gets nothing. Part 1 throws the IllegalStateException above, right after registered. Parts 2 to 4 each print unregistered: after take(2) with the first two readings, before the collector catches IOException: probe connection lost, and when the flow completes with the last reading. Part 5 shows trySend on a closed channel: isSuccess=false isClosed=true. With awaitRegistered(), part 0 prints registered, then fired with listeners=1 and got ProbeEvent(seq=0, celsius=61). The Java twin registers inside subscribe(), so its part 0 gets the reading at once, and its part 1 still has listeners=1 after take(1), with no error at all.

video.title: callbackFlow is a mailbox bolted to the SDK: the listener drops events in with trySend, awaitClose unregisters it, a burst of 200 gets 64 slots plus one waiting hand, and in tests advanceTimeBy(100) stops just before a task due at 100

sections.h: A burst of 200 on connect: 64 spots and one waiting hand
sections.html:
The probe keeps its readings while nobody listens, and on connect it replays them in one burst, from its own thread, one callback after another. Fire 200 readings into a default callbackFlow while its collector waits in receive(), and 135 trySend calls fail. The other 65 got through: 64 onto the shelf (Channel.BUFFERED), and one handed straight to the receiver that was already waiting, before the shelf was touched. So a shelf of 64 takes 65 when someone is waiting at the hatch. Better to know that before a test counts it for you.

trySend returns a ChannelResult that says whether it worked. Ignore it, and the 135 failures are silent losses. After the channel is closed it fails too, with isClosed=true. The fix is a policy you choose on purpose. A buffer(...) or conflate() right after callbackFlow { } fuses into its one channel (the shelves snapping together from Buffering), so it changes that channel instead of adding a second one:

After callbackFlow { } trySend failures The collector got
nothing (64, SUSPEND) 135 65 accepted
.buffer(Channel.UNLIMITED) 0 all 200
.conflate() 0 [0, 199]: the first went to the waiting receiver, the last stayed in the one spot
.buffer(10, DROP_OLDEST) 0 [0, 190, 191, ..., 199]
Java
// Java equivalent: Flux.create buffers without limit by default (OverflowStrategy.BUFFER);
// onBackpressureBuffer(500) caps it and fails with an overflow error past 500
Flux<ProbeReading> readings = Flux.create(sink -> { /* register, sink.next, onDispose */ })
    .onBackpressureBuffer(500);
Kotlin
fun FakeProbe.readings(): Flow<ProbeReading> = callbackFlow { /* register, trySend, awaitClose */ }
    .buffer(500)   // fused: the bridge's own channel now holds the 500 stored readings

trySendBlocking(e) looks like the safe version. It is trySend with a fallback of runBlocking { send(e) }, so when the shelf is full it blocks the probe's own thread until there is room. With the probe's thread pushing 200 readings and a collector that takes 2 ms each, trySend let the thread finish in about 1 ms and lost 135, while trySendBlocking lost none and held the probe's thread for about 340 ms. (That run uses the real clock, so your numbers will differ.) Use it only when the library runs your callback on a worker thread of its own, and making that thread wait is how you slow it down. Pick UNLIMITED only when the producer is known to stop. For a feed where only the latest value matters, conflate() drops readings in a way you can explain.

A failed trySend is a lost reading. Size the shelf for the burst, or choose what to drop.

Check yourself: what does the collector get from the same burst after .buffer(10, DROP_LATEST)? The probe now feeds a flow without losing anything. The neighbour wants the readings too, and her kitchen speaks Reactor.

REAL time. private fun probeThread(blocking: Boolean): Flow<Int> = callbackFlow { var failed = 0 val probe = thread(name = "probe-io") { val t0 = System.nanoTime() repeat(200) { if (blocking) trySendBlocking(it) else if (trySend(it).isFailure) failed++ } println(" probe thread done after ${(System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000} ms, trySend failures=$failed") channel.close() } awaitClose { probe.join() } } fun main() = runBlocking { println("== 1. a burst of 200 callbacks before the collector can run") println(" default buffer (64, SUSPEND):"); println(" collector got ${burst(200).take(64).count()}, then cancelled") println(" buffer(Channel.UNLIMITED):"); println(" collector got ${burst(200).buffer(Channel.UNLIMITED).take(200).count()}") println(" conflate():"); println(" collector got ${burst(200).conflate().take(2).toList()}") println(" buffer(10, DROP_OLDEST):"); println(" collector got ${burst(200).buffer(10, BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST).take(11).toList()}") println("== 2. the probe's own thread, collector takes 2 ms per reading (REAL time, numbers vary)") for (blocking in listOf(false, true)) { println(" ${if (blocking) "trySendBlocking" else "trySend"} into the default buffer:") println(" collector received ${probeThread(blocking).onEach { delay(2) }.count()}") } }

In part 2, trySend lets the probe's thread finish almost at once with about 135 failures, and the collector receives about 65. trySendBlocking holds the probe's thread for about 300 ms or more and loses nothing. sections.h: Across the Reactor bridge, demand becomes suspension
sections.html:
Reactor follows Reactive Streams, a small standard set of Java interfaces for streams, and it makes the subscriber say how much it can take, with request(n). That number is called demand. A Flow has no such call: it suspends. The bridges in the kotlinx-coroutines-reactive and kotlinx-coroutines-reactor modules translate one into the other.

Publisher.asFlow() works like a diner with an order pad, sitting at the end of the neighbour's line of stations. It orders 64, eats them, and orders 64 more after every 64 it has passed on. (A Flux is a Publisher, so flux.asFlow() is this same function.) The items wait in a channel of that size, and buffer sets the size of the order:

Flow side Requests sent to a 300-item Flux
asFlow() 64 after 0, 64, 128, 192 and 256
asFlow().buffer(10) 10 every 10
asFlow().buffer(0) 1 every 1
asFlow().conflate() or .buffer(UNLIMITED) Long.MAX_VALUE, once
asFlow().take(3) 64, then cancel: the 61 extra already in the channel are thrown away

That is a refill in batches. Reactor's own operators top up earlier: publishOn asked a Flow-backed Flux for 256 and then 192 at a time, and limitRate(10) for 10 and then 8.

Flow.asFlux() and asPublisher() go the other way. Nothing runs until the first request(n). Then each emit calls onNext right there, inside emit, and counts the demand down. When it reaches 0, the flow suspends inside that emit, and a later request resumes it. After request(2) the subscriber had [1, 2], and emit had returned only for 1: the flow was parked inside emit(2). Cancelling the subscription cancels the flow's coroutine, so a callbackFlow underneath runs its awaitClose.

Two details bite in real programs. The bridge runs the flow on Dispatchers.Unconfined unless you pass a dispatcher (the part that picks the thread a coroutine runs on), so the flow and every Reactor operator after it run on whichever thread resumed it: the subscriber's thread at first, kotlinx.coroutines.DefaultExecutor after a delay, and the probe's own thread under a probe bridge. Pass asFlux(dispatcher), or add publishOn before anything slow downstream. And Reactor's Context, a small map of values that travels with a subscription, crosses in both directions. Through asFlux(), a table number written with contextWrite was visible inside the flow as a ReactorContext element. The other way, a ReactorContext in the coroutine reaches a publisher collected with asFlow() only when kotlinx-coroutines-reactor is on the classpath, the list of libraries the program can see, because that module supplies the piece that injects it, found with ServiceLoader.

Java can't call Flow.collect, which it sees as Object collect(FlowCollector, Continuation). Give Java a face built in Kotlin:

Java
// Java caller: only Reactor types, no Flow and no Continuation
List<ProbeReading> firstTwo = new ProbeApi(probe).readingsFlux().take(2).collectList().block();
Kotlin
class ProbeApi(private val probe: FakeProbe) {
    fun readings(): Flow<ProbeReading> = probe.readings()          // for Kotlin callers
    fun readingsFlux(): Flux<ProbeReading> = readings().asFlux()   // for Java and Reactor callers
}

For a single result, a CompletableFuture built with scope.future { } is the better face, as lesson 11 of the coroutines track showed.

Give Java a Flux or a future, never a Flow.

Check yourself: how many requests does asFlow().buffer(10) send to a 300-item Flux, and why one more than 30? Every bridge in this lesson has a timing story, and testing timing on a real clock is slow and flaky. So the house rehearses.

Flux -> Flow: the collector's demand becomes request(n)") demand("asFlow()") { it.asFlow().collect { } } demand("asFlow().buffer(10)") { it.asFlow().buffer(10).collect { } } demand("asFlow().buffer(0)") { it.asFlow().buffer(0).take(3).collect { } } demand("asFlow().conflate()") { it.asFlow().conflate().collect { } } demand("asFlow().buffer(UNLIMITED)") { it.asFlow().buffer(Channel.UNLIMITED).collect { } } demand("asFlow().take(3)") { it.asFlow().take(3).collect { } } println("== 2. Flow -> Flux: the flow suspends inside emit when the demand runs out") val returned = mutableListOf<Int>() val received = mutableListOf<Int>() lateinit var subscription: Subscription PlateFaces.platesTracked(returned).subscribe(object : BaseSubscriber<Int>() { override fun hookOnSubscribe(s: Subscription) { subscription = s; s.request(2) } override fun hookOnNext(v: Int) { received += v } }) println(" after request(2): received=$received, emit() returned for $returned") subscription.request(3) println(" after request(3): received=$received, emit() returned for $returned") subscription.cancel() println("== 3. threads: asFlux() runs the flow on Dispatchers.Unconfined") val threads: Flow<String> = flow { emit("before delay: " + Thread.currentThread().name) delay(10) emit("after delay: " + Thread.currentThread().name) } threads.asFlux().map { "$it | onNext on " + Thread.currentThread().name }.collectList().block()!!.forEach { println(" $it") } println("== 4. context: a Reactor Context reaches the flow as ReactorContext") val table = flow { emit(currentCoroutineContext()[ReactorContext]?.context?.getOrDefault("table", "none") ?: "no ReactorContext") } println(" with contextWrite: " + table.asFlux().contextWrite(Context.of("table", "table-7")).blockFirst()) println(" without: " + table.asFlux().blockFirst()) }

sections.h: The test clock has edges: where runCurrent, advanceTimeBy and advanceUntilIdle stop
sections.html:
runTest is the rehearsal dinner from lesson 10 of the coroutines track. It replaces the clock with a scheduler that jumps from one due task to the next, so a delay takes no real time: that fake clock is virtual time. Three calls move it along, and each one stops in a different place:

  • runCurrent() runs everything that is due now.
  • advanceTimeBy(n) runs ahead up to, but not including, now + n. With tasks due at 100 and 200, advanceTimeBy(100) leaves the clock at 100 with fired=[]. Only runCurrent() then runs the task at 100.
  • advanceUntilIdle() runs ahead until only background work is left. With nothing but a poller in backgroundScope, it leaves t=0 polls=0, while advanceTimeBy(5000) plus runCurrent() gives t=5000 polls=5.

backgroundScope is a scope inside runTest for coroutines that never end on their own; they are cancelled when the test body ends. A test that collects a hot flow there should drive the clock with advanceTimeBy(...) and runCurrent(), as this track's labs do. Reactor's virtual clock puts the edge elsewhere:

Java
// Java equivalent: Reactor's VirtualTimeScheduler includes the end point
@Test
void taskDueAt100RunsWithAdvanceTimeBy() {
    VirtualTimeScheduler clock = VirtualTimeScheduler.create();
    List<Long> fired = new ArrayList<>();
    clock.schedule(() -> fired.add(100L), 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
    clock.advanceTimeBy(Duration.ofMillis(100));
    assertThat(fired).containsExactly(100L);  // already ran, no extra step
}
Kotlin
@Test
fun `the task due at 100 needs runCurrent`() = runTest {
    val fired = mutableListOf<Long>()
    launch { delay(100); fired += currentTime }
    advanceTimeBy(100)
    assertThat(fired).isEmpty()               // runs only what is due BEFORE now + 100
    runCurrent()
    assertThat(fired).containsExactly(100L)   // runs what is due now
}

The test dispatcher decides what a StateFlow collector sees. A dish tracker's cookAndServe() sets COOKING and then SERVED, with no suspension between them. A collector on the default StandardTestDispatcher runs only when the test lets the clock move, so it saw [ORDERED, SERVED]. One launched with UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler), which runs a coroutine at once, inside the call that wakes it, saw all three. That dispatcher is experimental. A real collector on Dispatchers.Default, which runs coroutines on real threads, can see either. So the Unconfined test shows the most a collector can see, and the Standard one shows the menu board skipping a value. Assert on the final state and on the changes that matter. If every change matters, the type shouldn't be a StateFlow.

Two failures come with exact messages. async { status.take(3).toList() } waits for a third value that the board skipped, and with runTest(timeout = 500.milliseconds) it ends in UncompletedCoroutinesError: After waiting for 500ms, the test body did not run to completion. (The default timeout is 60 s, and the 20 s JUnit timeout in these labs fires first.) A hot flow collected in the test scope itself, or stateIn(this, WhileSubscribed(), 0), fails with there were active child jobs, followed by the advice to use TestScope.backgroundScope.

advanceTimeBy(n) stops just before n. Follow it with runCurrent().

Check yourself: change advanceTimeBy(100) to advanceTimeBy(101) in the first part of the Try it. What does its first line print? Driving the clock by hand is precise and a little tedious. A library can read the flow for you, and its one blind spot is worth knowing.

_status.value = "SERVED" } // no suspension between } // The edges of the test clock. runTest is called from main here; in a test it is the body. @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun main() { runTest { println("== 1. advanceTimeBy(n) runs what is due BEFORE now + n") val fired = mutableListOf<Long>() launch { delay(100); fired += currentTime } launch { delay(200); fired += currentTime } advanceTimeBy(100); println(" after advanceTimeBy(100): t=$currentTime fired=$fired") runCurrent(); println(" after runCurrent(): t=$currentTime fired=$fired") advanceUntilIdle(); println(" after advanceUntilIdle(): t=$currentTime fired=$fired") } runTest { println("== 2. advanceUntilIdle() stops once only backgroundScope work is left") var polls = 0 backgroundScope.launch { while (true) { delay(1_000); polls++ } } // a poller that never ends, like a thermometer advanceUntilIdle(); println(" after advanceUntilIdle(): t=$currentTime polls=$polls") advanceTimeBy(5_000); runCurrent(); println(" after advanceTimeBy(5000) + runCurrent(): t=$currentTime polls=$polls") } runTest { println("== 3. a StateFlow set twice in a row, collected two ways") val a = DishTracker(); val standard = mutableListOf<String>() backgroundScope.launch { a.status.toList(standard) } runCurrent(); a.cookAndServe(); runCurrent() val b = DishTracker(); val unconfined = mutableListOf<String>() backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { b.status.toList(unconfined) } b.cookAndServe() println(" Standard collector: $standard") println(" Unconfined collector: $unconfined") } println("== 4. take(3) on that StateFlow (runTest timeout 500 ms of REAL time)") try { runTest(timeout = 500.milliseconds) { val t = DishTracker() val three = async { t.status.take(3).toList() } runCurrent() t.cookAndServe() println(" got ${three.await()}") } } catch (e: Throwable) { println(" ${e::class.qualifiedName}: ${e.message?.lines()?.first()}") } println("== 5. stateIn(this, WhileSubscribed()) inside runTest, over flowOf(1, 2, 3)") try { runTest(timeout = 500.milliseconds) { val s = flowOf(1, 2, 3).stateIn(this, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(), 0) println(" saw ${s.first { it == 3 }}, test body done") } println(" test passed") } catch (e: Throwable) { println(" ${e::class.qualifiedName}: ${e.message?.lines()?.first()?.replace(Regex("@[0-9a-f]+"), "@...")}") } }

try.expect: Part 1: t=100 fired=[], then fired=[100] after runCurrent(), then t=200 fired=[100, 200]. Part 2: t=0 polls=0, then t=5000 polls=5. Part 3: [ORDERED, SERVED] for the Standard collector and [ORDERED, COOKING, SERVED] for the Unconfined one. Part 4: UncompletedCoroutinesError: After waiting for 500ms, the test body did not run to completion. Part 5 prints saw 3, test body done and then fails with there were active child jobs, because the WhileSubscribed sharing coroutine never ends. With advanceTimeBy(101) the clock stops at 101 and the task at 100 has already run, so the first line reads t=101 fired=[100]. (Reactor's virtual clock has no Java twin here: it lives in reactor-test, which only the tests can use.)

sections.h: Turbine writes down every value, and that is its blind spot
sections.html:
Turbine 1.2.1 (app.cash.turbine, a test dependency of this lab module) is a test library that turns a flow into a list of events you read one by one:

Java
// Java equivalent: StepVerifier subscribes, then runs each step in order
StepVerifier.create(api.readingsFlux())
    .then(() -> probe.fire(first))
    .expectNext(first)
    .then(() -> probe.fail(new IOException("probe connection lost")))
    .expectErrorMessage("probe connection lost")
    .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(5));
Kotlin
probe.readings().test {          // collects before the block runs: the listener is registered
    probe.fire(first)
    assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo(first)
    probe.fail(IOException("probe connection lost"))
    assertThat(awaitError()).hasMessage("probe connection lost")
}

Picture the rehearsal's note-taker. test { } runs the flow up to its first suspension before your block starts, so a SharedFlow is subscribed and a callbackFlow listener is registered by then, which removes the race from the first section. Every event goes into her notebook, an unlimited channel, in order. You read it with awaitItem(), awaitComplete() and awaitError(), which hands you the error as an event instead of throwing it. An event you never read fails the test with Unconsumed events found, unless you end with cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents(). If no new event arrives within 3 s of real time, the test fails with No value produced in 3s. The flow's own delay calls stay virtual inside runTest; only Turbine's wait is real. To follow two flows at once, call testIn(backgroundScope) inside turbineScope { }. Outside it, testIn compiles and then fails at run time with Turbine can only collect flows within a TurbineContext.

The note-taker hears everything, and that is her blind spot. Turbine collects on UnconfinedTestDispatcher, so it takes each value the instant it is sent. It saw COOKING, which the Standard collector of the last section never got. It also took all 500 readings of a burst through a 64-spot callbackFlow, where a Standard collector got 65. She never misses a word, which makes her a poor witness to what a slower listener would miss.

So use Turbine to check what a flow emits and in what order. Don't use it to test skipped values, buffer sizes or a slow collector. For those, collect with a Standard collector in backgroundScope and drive the clock yourself, as the lab's burst test does. And on a SharedFlow with no replay, a value emitted before test { } starts is gone, so the test fails with No value produced.

Turbine shows what a flow says, not what a slow listener hears. Test buffers with a Standard collector.

Check yourself: which test in the lab would still pass with a 64-spot buffer if you rewrote it with Turbine, and why? Every bridge in this lesson sits on top of something that waits: a probe's thread, a Reactor line, a clock. Underneath them all is the place where waiting really happens.

Read each one, predict the commented line, then run the class. */ @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) // TestScope.runCurrent is experimental in 1.11.0 class TurbineTourTest { @Test fun `1 items and completion are awaited in order`() = runTest { flowOf("COOKING", "SERVED").test { assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo("COOKING") assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo("SERVED") awaitComplete() } } @Test fun `2 an event you did not read fails the test`() = runTest { val failure = runCatching { flowOf("one", "two").test { awaitItem() } }.exceptionOrNull() assertThat(failure).hasMessageContaining("Unconsumed events found") // lists Item(two) and Complete } @Test fun `3 an error arrives as an event, not as a thrown exception`() = runTest { flow { emit(1); throw IOException("probe lost") }.test { assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo(1) assertThat(awaitError()).hasMessage("probe lost") } } @Test fun `4 Turbine sees every StateFlow value, a Standard collector does not`() = runTest { val tracker = TourTracker() tracker.status.test { assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo("ORDERED") tracker.cookAndServe() assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo("COOKING") // Turbine collects on UnconfinedTestDispatcher assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo("SERVED") } val other = TourTracker() val seen = mutableListOf<String>() backgroundScope.launch { other.status.toList(seen) } // StandardTestDispatcher, closer to production runCurrent() other.cookAndServe() runCurrent() assertThat(seen).containsExactly("ORDERED", "SERVED") } @Test fun `5 Turbine never lets a callbackFlow buffer fill`() = runTest { val probe = FakeProbe() val defaultBuffer: Flow<ProbeReading> = callbackFlow { // 64 slots, as callbackFlow has by default val r = probe.register(object : ProbeListener { override fun onReading(reading: ProbeReading) { trySend(reading) } override fun onError(error: Throwable) { close(error) } override fun onClosed() { close() } }) awaitClose { r.unregister() } } defaultBuffer.test { probe.burst(500) repeat(500) { awaitItem() } // all 500 arrive: each one was taken the moment it was sent cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents() } val seen = mutableListOf<ProbeReading>() backgroundScope.launch { defaultBuffer.collect { seen += it } } runCurrent() probe.burst(500) runCurrent() assertThat(seen).hasSize(65) // a Standard collector: 64 buffered plus 1 handed straight over } @Test fun `6 a SharedFlow value emitted before test {} is lost`() = runTest { val events = MutableSharedFlow<String>() events.emit("SERVED") // nobody is subscribed yet, and replay = 0 val failure = runCatching { events.test(timeout = 500.milliseconds) { awaitItem() } }.exceptionOrNull() assertThat(failure).hasMessage("No value produced in 500ms") // after 500 ms of REAL time } @Test fun `7 the flow's delays are virtual, Turbine's timeout is wall-clock`() = runTest { flow { delay(10.seconds); emit("late") }.test(timeout = 200.milliseconds) { assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo("late") awaitComplete() } } @Test fun `8 several flows at once with turbineScope and testIn`() = runTest { turbineScope { val readings = flowOf(180, 181).testIn(backgroundScope, name = "readings") val alerts = flowOf("door open").testIn(backgroundScope, name = "alerts") assertThat(readings.awaitItem()).isEqualTo(180) assertThat(alerts.awaitItem()).isEqualTo("door open") assertThat(readings.awaitItem()).isEqualTo(181) readings.awaitComplete() alerts.awaitComplete() } } }

java.html: static Flux<ProbeReading> readings(FakeProbe probe) { return Flux.<ProbeReading>create(sink -> { Registration registration = probe.register(new ProbeListener() { @Override public void onReading(ProbeReading r) { sink.next(r); } // runs the subscriber inline @Override public void onError(Throwable t) { sink.error(t); } @Override public void onClosed() { sink.complete(); } }); sink.onDispose(registration::unregister); // optional: nothing complains if it is missing }) .onBackpressureBuffer(500); // the default buffer has no limit }

kotlin.title: ProbeReadings.kt (callbackFlow)
kotlin.html: fun FakeProbe.readings(): Flow<ProbeReading> = callbackFlow { val registration = register(object : ProbeListener { override fun onReading(reading: ProbeReading) { trySend(reading) } // never blocks the probe's thread override fun onError(error: Throwable) { close(error) } override fun onClosed() { close() } }) awaitClose { registration.unregister() } // required: collecting throws without it }.buffer(500) // fused into the bridge's channel; the default is 64

compare.note: The shapes match line for line, and four things differ. Registration time: Flux.create registers inside subscribe(), while callbackFlow registers when its producer coroutine first runs, so a reading fired right after collect starts can be lost. Cleanup: callbackFlow throws when its block returns without awaitClose, and Reactor lets a missing onDispose leak the listener with no message. Buffering: Kotlin's channel holds 64 (65 with a waiting receiver) and makes you look at trySend's result; Reactor buffers without limit unless you add a policy. Threads: sink.next calls the subscriber's onNext on the probe's thread, while the Kotlin collector runs on its own dispatcher and the probe's thread only drops the reading into the channel. That holds until you turn the flow into a Flux with plain asFlux(), whose Unconfined default puts the subscriber back on the probe's thread.

worked.title: Hand the probe to Java, and test it from both sides

steps.say: Start from the Kotlin bridge, the lab's solution. It registers per collector, never blocks the probe's thread, closes the channel on onError and onClosed, and has room for the 500 stored readings.
steps.code: fun FakeProbe.readings(): Flow<ProbeReading> = callbackFlow { val registration = register(object : ProbeListener { override fun onReading(reading: ProbeReading) { trySend(reading) } // 1. hand over, never block override fun onError(error: Throwable) { close(error) } // 2. fail the flow override fun onClosed() { close() } // 3. complete it }) awaitClose { registration.unregister() } // 4. clean up on any ending }.buffer(500)

alt.html: // Java equivalent of the same four steps static Flux<ProbeReading> readings(FakeProbe probe) { return Flux.<ProbeReading>create(sink -> { Registration registration = probe.register(new ProbeListener() { @Override public void onReading(ProbeReading r) { sink.next(r); } // 1. @Override public void onError(Throwable t) { sink.error(t); } // 2. @Override public void onClosed() { sink.complete(); } // 3. }); sink.onDispose(registration::unregister); // 4. }).onBackpressureBuffer(500); }

steps.say: Give Java a face. asFlux() starts the flow at the first request(n), so registration happens then and not at subscribe(). A cancelled subscription cancels the flow, so awaitClose unregisters.
steps.code: class ProbeApi(private val probe: FakeProbe) { fun readings(): Flow<ProbeReading> = probe.readings() fun readingsFlux(): Flux<ProbeReading> = probe.readings().asFlux() // Unconfined: pass a dispatcher if operators after it are slow }

alt.html: // what the Java caller writes: Reactor types only List<ProbeReading> firstTwo = new ProbeApi(probe).readingsFlux().take(2).collectList().block();

steps.say: Test the content with Turbine and the buffer with a Standard collector. Turbine registers before its block runs and reads events in order. The burst test needs a collector that can't run during the burst, so it uses the default dispatcher and runCurrent().
steps.code: @Test fun `a probe error fails the flow`() = runTest { probe.readings().test { probe.fire(first) assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo(first) probe.fail(IOException("probe connection lost")) assertThat(awaitError()).hasMessage("probe connection lost") } } @Test fun `a 500-reading burst arrives in full`() = runTest { val got = mutableListOf<ProbeReading>() backgroundScope.launch { probe.readings().collect { got += it } } runCurrent() // registered and waiting probe.burst(500) // 500 synchronous callbacks runCurrent() assertThat(got).hasSize(500) }

alt.html: // the Java side, with StepVerifier: no demand at first, so nothing is registered yet StepVerifier.create(api.readingsFlux(), 0) .then(() -> assertThat(probe.getListenerCount()).isZero()) .thenRequest(1) .then(() -> probe.fire(first)) .expectNext(first) .thenCancel() .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(5)); assertThat(probe.getListenerCount()).isZero(); // cancel reached awaitClose

steps.say: Self-check: why does the burst test avoid Turbine, which would make it shorter? (Turbine collects on UnconfinedTestDispatcher, so every trySend wakes it at once and the reading leaves the channel immediately. The buffer never fills, and a 64-spot version would pass with all 500 readings. In the tour test, a Standard collector got 65.)

lab.title: Bridge the probe's listener, hand it to Java, test it both ways
steps: Run the tests. The five ProbeReadingsTest cases and the three in ProbeFluxTest (a Java test) fail. TurbineTourTest and StepVerifierTourTest already pass: they are this lesson's Try it. Read one failure: it is the awaitClose message from the first section.

In ProbeReadings.kt, keep the Registration that register returns, close the channel from onError and onClosed, and end the block with awaitClose. Run ProbeReadingsTest. One test still fails, with a number you have seen in this lesson.
Size the bridge's channel for the 500 stored readings that the KDoc promises, without blocking the probe's thread.
In ProbeApi.kt, write readingsFlux(). Run ProbeFluxTest, which sees only Reactor types.
Run all the l08 tests. Then read ProbeReadingsTest and say, for each test, why it uses Turbine, an Unconfined collector or a Standard one.
hints: close(error) and close() belong to the ProducerScope the block runs in, so you can call them from inside the listener object.

Expected size: 500 but was: 65 is the default 64 spots plus the one reading handed to the waiting collector. A buffer(...) right after callbackFlow { } is fused into its channel. Channel.UNLIMITED passes too; a number states how much memory you allow.
Don't reach for trySendBlocking. In the burst test the probe's thread is the test's only thread, the one the collector needs in order to run.
asFlux() is in kotlinx.coroutines.reactor. It starts the flow at the first request(n) and cancels it when the subscription is cancelled, which is what the Java tests check.
lab.done: All tests in workbench.flows.l08 pass: ProbeReadingsTest, ProbeFluxTest and the two tours.

drill.title: A listener bridge, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. A made-up kitchen scale library has fun subscribe(onWeight: (Weight) -> Unit, onFailure: (Throwable) -> Unit): Cancellable. Write fun KitchenScale.weights(): Flow<Weight> that never blocks the scale's thread, fails the flow on onFailure, holds a burst of 1,000 weights, and cancels the subscription whatever ends the collection. Then say in a comment what happens if you leave out the cleanup line.

answer.html: fun KitchenScale.weights(): Flow<Weight> = callbackFlow { val subscription = subscribe( onWeight = { weight -> trySend(weight) }, // never blocks the scale's thread onFailure = { error -> close(error) }, // collect throws this error ) awaitClose { subscription.cancel() } // on take(n), cancellation, close and error }.buffer(1_000) // fused into the callbackFlow's channel // Without awaitClose the block returns with the channel open, and collecting throws // IllegalStateException: 'awaitClose { yourCallbackOrListener.cancel() }' should be used // in the end of callbackFlow block.

alt.title: Java equivalent
alt.html: // Java equivalent, for a library whose Java API is subscribe(Consumer<Weight>, Consumer<Throwable>) Flux<Weight> weights(KitchenScale scale) { return Flux.<Weight>create(sink -> { Cancellable subscription = scale.subscribe(sink::next, sink::error); sink.onDispose(subscription::cancel); // leave it out and the subscription leaks, silently }).onBackpressureBuffer(1_000); // caps the default unlimited buffer }

recap: callbackFlow registers when its producer coroutine first runs, after collect starts, so a value fired in between is lost. Tests wait for the registration; Turbine's test { } does it for you. Reactor's Flux.create registers inside subscribe().

awaitClose { unregister() } runs on take(n), cancellation, close(error) and close(). Without it, collecting throws the exact IllegalStateException shown in the lesson. Use channelFlow for your own coroutines and suspendCancellableCoroutine for a callback that fires once.

The bridge holds 64 by default plus one handed to a waiting receiver, so 65 of a 200-reading burst got in. Check trySend's result, and choose a fused buffer(n), conflate() or UNLIMITED (for a producer known to stop) on purpose. trySendBlocking blocks the library's thread.

Publisher.asFlow() requests 64, then 64 more after each 64; buffer(n) makes it request(n). asFlux() starts at the first request, calls onNext inside emit and suspends there when demand runs out, on Unconfined unless you pass a dispatcher. Give Java a Flux or a CompletableFuture, never a Flow.

advanceTimeBy(n) runs what is due before now + n, runCurrent() what is due now, and advanceUntilIdle() stops when only backgroundScope work is left. Turbine reads a flow in order with a 3 s real-time timeout, but it collects on UnconfinedTestDispatcher, so test skipped values and buffer sizes with a Standard collector.
The limit: these bridges and tests live inside one program, on top of threads and sockets that do the real waiting. How that waiting scales is the next track's subject.

explain.prompt: Explain to a friend why probe.fire(r) right after backgroundScope.launch { probe.readings().collect { ... } } loses the reading in a test, why rewriting the test with Turbine fixes that, and why Turbine would then hide a buffer that is too small.
explain.answer: On the default StandardTestDispatcher, launch only queues the collector. The callbackFlow's producer coroutine, which calls register, runs the next time the scheduler runs, so the fire happens with no listener and the reading goes nowhere. Turbine's test { } runs the flow up to its first suspension before the block starts, so by then the listener is registered. But Turbine collects on UnconfinedTestDispatcher. Each trySend wakes it at once and the reading leaves the channel right away, so the channel never fills, and a 64-spot buffer passes a 500-reading burst. To test the buffer, collect with a Standard collector that can't run during the burst: launch it, call runCurrent() so it registers, fire the burst, call runCurrent() again and count.

deeper.html:
The JDK has its own Reactive Streams interfaces, java.util.concurrent.Flow, with Publisher, Subscriber and Subscription. kotlinx.coroutines bridges them in a separate artifact, org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-jdk9:1.11.0. It is a thin wrapper over the reactive module: asFlow(), asPublisher() and collect for the JDK types, with the same demand mapping (a JDK publisher over 150 items saw request(64) three times). You don't need the extra artifact. reactive-streams 1.0.4, already on this lab's classpath through kotlinx-coroutines-reactive, has org.reactivestreams.FlowAdapters, and FlowAdapters.toPublisher(jdkPublisher).asFlow() does the same job.

The JDK HttpClient shows why that matters. client.sendAsync(request, BodyHandlers.ofPublisher()) is two bridges in one call. The CompletableFuture completes once, when the headers arrive, so it belongs to await(). The body is a JDK Flow.Publisher<List<ByteBuffer>> that delivers chunks as they come off the socket, so it belongs to asFlow(). In one run against a local server that wrote five lines 50 ms apart, the chunks arrived about 50 ms apart too. Wrapping the future in callbackFlow would be the wrong tool: a single result is a suspendCancellableCoroutine or await() job.

A few facts about the Reactor modules themselves. The README of kotlinx-coroutines-reactive calls asPublisher TCK-compliant, meaning it passes the official Reactive Streams compatibility tests. The subscription it creates has no parent job, so its lifetime belongs to the subscription and not to any scope. Element types must be non-null (T : Any), because Reactive Streams forbids null items. And the 1.11.0 reactor module declares reactor-core 3.4.1 in its pom; this course pins 3.8.8, and Gradle picks the higher version.
